sections.title: A open set characterization of continuity
A closed set characterization of continuity

excerpts.label: Definition 3.1 (Topological Space)

fullSourceSegments.text:
Definition 3.1 (Topological Space). A topology on a set X is a family τ of
subsets of X (called open sets) satisfying:
    1. Both ∅ and X belong to τ ;
                                                                            S
    2. Arbitrary unions of sets in τ belong to τ : if {Ui }i∈I ⊆ τ , then        i∈I Ui ∈ τ ;
                                                                                 Tn
    3. Finite intersections of sets in τ belong to τ : if {Vj }nj=1 ⊆ τ , then     j=1 Vj ∈
       τ.
The pair (X, τ ) is called a topological space. In many cases, we will omit the
mention of the topology and simply refer to the space X.

excerpts.label: Definition 3.2
excerpts.text: Let (X, τ) be a topological space. A subset A ⊆ X is called closed if its complement X ∖ A is open, i.e., X ∖ A ∈ τ.

fullSourceSegments.text:
Definition 3.2. Let (X, τ ) be a topological space. A subset A ⊆ X is called
closed if its complement X \ A is open, i.e., X \ A ∈ τ .

excerpts.text: Suppose (X, τ) is a topological space and let A be a subset of X. The subspace topology on A is the collection τ_{A} := {U ∩ A : U ∈ τ}. Then (A, τ_{A}) is a topological space.

excerpts.label: Definition 3.55
excerpts.text: A function f : (X, τ_{X}) → (Y, τ_{Y}) between topological spaces is called continuous at a given point x ∈ X if for every neighbourhood V of f(x) in Y, there exists a neighbourhood U of x in X such that f(U) ⊆ V. We say that f is continuous if it is continuous at every point x ∈ X.

fullSourceSegments.text:
Definition 3.55. A function f : (X, τX ) → (Y, τY ) between topological spaces
is called continuous at a given point x ∈ X if for every neighbourhood V of
f (x) in Y , there exists a neighbourhood U of x in X such that f (U ) ⊆ V . We
say that f is continuous if it is continuous at every point x ∈ X.

excerpts.label: Theorem 3.57
excerpts.text:
Let X and Y be topological spaces and let f : X → Y be a function. The following are equivalent:
1. f is continuous.
2. For all open sets H in Y, f^{−1}(H) is open in X.
3. For all closed sets C in Y, f^{−1}(C) is closed in X.
4. For all A ⊂ X, f(‾{A}) ⊆ ‾{f(A)} (This can be thought of as the Kuratowski definition of continuity).

excerpts.label: Theorem 3.64, item 4
excerpts.text: (Restricting the domain) If f : X → Y is continuous and A ⊆ X, then the restriction f|_{A} : A → Y defined by f|_{A}(a) = f(a) is continuous.

excerpts.label: Definition 3.69
excerpts.text: A function f : X → Y between topological spaces is a homeomorphism if it is a bijection and both f and f^{−1} are continuous.

excerpts.label: Definition 3.69
excerpts.text:
Definition 3.69. A function f : X → Y between topological spaces is a home-
omorphism if it is a bijection and both f and f −1 are continuous.
   If f is not surjective, we let Z = f (X). If the restriction f ′ : X → Z is a
homeomorphism, then we say that f is a topological embedding of X into Y .
    Homeomorphisms preserve topological properties, meaning that if X and Y
are homeomorphic, they share all topological characteristics. More precisely, we
have the following theorem.

excerpts.label: Example 3.74 (Continuous bijection not a homeomorphism)
excerpts.text:
Let X = [0, 1) with the usual topology from ℝ, and Y = S^{1} = {(x, y) ∈ ℝ^{2} : x^{2} + y^{2} = 1} with the subspace topology from ℝ^{2}. Define f : X → Y, f(t) = (cos 2πt, sin 2πt). Then f is a continuous bijection. However, f^{−1} is not continuous: around (1, 0) ∈ S^{1}, neighborhoods correspond to t near 0 and near 1, which are far apart in [0, 1), so f^{−1} fails continuity there.
This shows that a continuous bijection need not be a homeomorphism when the domain is not compact.

                                     X = [0, 1)

with the usual topology from R, and

                      Y = S 1 = {(x, y) ∈ R2 : x2 + y 2 = 1}

excerpts.text: A map is said to be open if the image of every open set is open. Similarly, a map is said to be closed if the image of every closed set is closed.

excerpts.label: Definition 5.18
excerpts.text: We say a topological space X is Hausdorff if for any two distinct points x, y ∈ X, there exist disjoint open sets U and V such that x ∈ U and y ∈ V.

fullSourceSegments.text:
Definition 5.18. We say a topological space X is Hausdorff if for any two
distinct points x, y ∈ X, there exist disjoint open sets U and V such that x ∈ U
and y ∈ V .

excerpts.label: Example 5.23
excerpts.text: Every metric space is Hausdorff. For x, y ∈ X with x ≠ y, let ε = d(x, y)/2 > 0. Then the open balls B_{ε}(x) and B_{ε}(y) are disjoint neighbourhoods of x and y, respectively.

excerpts.label: Definition 6.3
excerpts.text: A topological space X is compact if every open cover 𝒰 of X has a finite subcover, i.e., there exist finitely many U_{1}, U_{2}, …, U_{n} ∈ 𝒰 such that X ⊆ U_{1} ∪ U_{2} ∪ … ∪ U_{n}.

excerpts.label: Definition 6.56
excerpts.text: A space X is said to be compact if every open cover of X has a finite subcover.

fullSourceSegments.text:
Definition 6.56. A space X is said to be compact if every open cover of X has
a finite subcover.

It turns out that we can characterize compactness using refinements of open
covers.

excerpts.label: Just before Lemma 6.9
excerpts.text: We say a collection of sets {U_{α}} in X covers Y ⊂ X if Y ⊆ ⋃_{α} U_{α}.

excerpts.label: Lemma 6.9
excerpts.text: Y ⊂ X is compact iff every cover of Y by open sets in X has a finite subcover.

fullSourceSegments.text:

excerpts.label: Theorem 6.11
excerpts.text: Every closed subset Y of a compact space X is compact.

fullSourceSegments.text: Theorem 6.11. Every closed subset Y of a compact space X is compact.

excerpts.label: Theorem 6.12
excerpts.text: Every compact subspace Y of a Hausdorff space X is closed.

fullSourceSegments.text: Theorem 6.12. Every compact subspace Y of a Hausdorff space X is closed.

excerpts.text: If f : X → Y is continuous and X is compact, then f(X) is compact.

excerpts.label: Theorem 6.20
excerpts.text: Let f : X → Y be a bijective continuous map. Assume that X is compact and Y is Hausdorff. Then f is a homeomorphism.

Example 1.1. Some basic examples of sets include:
    • The natural numbers N = {1, 2, 3, . . .}

    • The integers Z = {. . . , −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, . . .}
    • The real numbers R

Set calculus A set A is a subset of a set B if every element of A is also an
element of B. We write A ⊆ B to denote that A is a subset of B. If A is a
subset of B but not equal to B, we say that A is a proper subset of B and denote
it by A ⊊ B.
    We let P(A) denote the power set of A, which is the set of all subsets of A.
    We say two sets A and B are equal if they have the same elements, that is,
if A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A. We write A = B to denote that A and B are equal.
    We let A\B denote the set difference of A and B, which is the set of elements
in A that are not in B. Formally, A\B = {x ∈ A : x ∈    / B}. When B ⊆ A, we
say A\B is the complement of B in A.
    The empty set, denoted ∅, is a set that contains no elements. It is a subset
of every set.

excerpts.label: Example 1.4
excerpts.text:
Example 1.4 (Russell’s paradox). Let P denote the set of all sets. Then, form
Q := {A ∈ P |A ∈
               / A}. Is Q ∈ Q?
   More axiomatic treatment of sets can be found in Zermelo-Fraenkel set the-
ory (ZF), which provides a formal foundation for set theory and avoids para-
doxes like Russell’s paradox by carefully restricting the kinds of sets that can
be formed. For example, under ZF axioms, the collection of all sets is not a set
but a proper class, because it violates one of the axioms requiring that a set
cannot contain itself as an element.

excerpts.label: Theorem 1.20
excerpts.text:
Theorem 1.20 (Partitions and equivalence relations). Let A be a nonempty set.
There is a one-to-one correspondence between partitions of A and equivalence
relations on A:
   • Define f : Part(A) → EqRel(A) by sending a partition {Ai }i∈I to the
     equivalence relation ∼ on A defined by a ∼ b if and only if ∃i ∈ I with
     a, b ∈ Ai .
   • Conversely, define g : EqRel(A) → Part(A) by sending an equivalence
     relation ∼ on A to the family of equivalence classes
                                                 {[a] : a ∈ A}
      which is a partition of A.
Then, f and g are bijections and they are inverse to each other, i.e.,
                        g ◦ f = idPart(A) ,            f ◦ g = idEqRel(A) .

excerpts.label: Example 1.22
excerpts.text:
Example 1.22. Consider the set of real numbers R with the usual order relation
≤. This is a partial order because it is reflexive (every number is less than or
equal to itself), antisymmetric (if a ≤ b and b ≤ a, then a = b), and transitive
(if a ≤ b and b ≤ c, then a ≤ c).
    Just a funny note: we humans know that 0.9 > 0.11 but somehow many
LLMs think 0.9 < 0.11. So be careful when using AIs in your studies :)

excerpts.label: Example 1.35
excerpts.text:
Example 1.35.         • We define the lexicographic order on N × N as follows:
    for (m1 , n1 ), (m2 , n2 ) ∈ N × N, we say that (m1 , n1 ) ≤ (m2 , n2 ) if either
    m1 < m2 or m1 = m2 and n1 ≤ n2 . Then, (N × N, ≤) is a well-ordered
    set.
   • We can similarly define the lexicographic order on Nk for any finite k ∈ N,
     which makes (Nk , ≤) a well-ordered set as well.
   • However, the lexicographic order on NN is not well-ordered: consider the
      subset B = {(2, 1, 1, . . .) > (1, 2, 1, . . .) > . . .}. Then, B has no minimal
      element.
   The lexicographic order on NN is not well-ordered. In fact, no one has found
an explicit well-order on NN so far. However, it turns out that in theory, one
can find a partial order on NN so that it is well-ordered.

    for (m1 , n1 ), (m2 , n2 ) ∈ N × N, we say that (m1 , n1 ) ≤ (m2 , n2 ) if either
    m1 < m2 or m1 = m2 and n1 ≤ n2 . Then, (N × N, ≤) is a well-ordered
    set.
   • We can similarly define the lexicographic order on Nk for any finite k ∈ N,
     which makes (Nk , ≤) a well-ordered set as well.
   • However, the lexicographic order on NN is not well-ordered: consider the
      subset B = {(2, 1, 1, . . .) > (1, 2, 1, . . .) > . . .}. Then, B has no minimal
      element.
   The lexicographic order on NN is not well-ordered. In fact, no one has found
an explicit well-order on NN so far. However, it turns out that in theory, one
can find a partial order on NN so that it is well-ordered.

excerpts.label: Theorem 1.51
excerpts.text:
Theorem 1.51. The following statements are equivalent:
  1. (Axiom of Choice) If {Ai }i∈I is a family of nonempty pairwise disjoint
     sets, there is a set B ⊂ ∪Ai such that B ∩ Ai is exactly one element for
     all i ∈ I.
  2. (Zorn’s Lemma) If each chain (linearly ordered set) in a nonempty poset
     A has an upper bound, then A has a maximal element.
  3. (Maximal Principle) In a poset, every chain is contained in a maximal
     chain.

  4. (Zermelo’s Well-Ordering Theorem) Every set can be well-ordered.

excerpts.label: Example 1.63
excerpts.text:
Example 1.63. The set of positive rational numbers Q+ is countably infinite.
We can enumerate it as follows: Represent each rational number as a pair
(m, n) ∈ N2 by the (not necessarily reduced) fraction m/n. Enumerate lattice
points by successive anti-diagonals in a zig-zag (Cantor) pattern:
                                1     2      3     4     5
                                5     5      5     5     5


                                1     2      3     4     5
                                4     4      4     4     4


                                1     2      3     4     5
                                3     3      3     3     3


                                1     2      3     4     5
                                2     2      2     2     2


                                1     2      3     4     5
                                1     1      1     1     1




Skipping repetitions (keep only reduced fractions) we obtain an enumeration of
Q+ , i.e., an bijection from Q+ to N. Therefore, |Q+ | = ℵ0 .
   Now let’s see some criteria for countability.

excerpts.label: Definition 2.1
excerpts.text:
Definition 2.1 (Metric Space). A metric space is a pair (X, d) consisting of a
set X and a function d : X × X → [0, ∞) called a metric such that
    1. d(x, y) = 0 if and only if x = y;
    2. d(x, y) = d(y, x) for all x, y ∈ X (symmetry);
    3. d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z) for all x, y, z ∈ X (triangle inequality).
The value d(x, y) is called the distance between points x and y in the metric
space.
   If (X, d) satisfies 2 and 3 and 1’ below, it is called a pseudometric space.
   1’. d(x, x) = 0 for all x ∈ X.

excerpts.text:
Example 2.2.         1. X = Rn , dp (x, y) = ∥x − y∥p = ( i=1 |xi − yi |p )     for
      1 ≤ p < ∞ and d∞ (x, y) = ∥x − y∥∞ = max1≤i≤n |xi − yi | are metrics on

excerpts.text:
Definition 2.3. Let (X, dX ) and (Y, dY ) be metric spaces. A function f : X →
Y is called an isometric embedding if

                  dY (f (x), f (x′ )) = dX (x, x′ )   for all x, x′ ∈ X.

The function f is called an isometry if it is an isometric embedding that is also
surjective and we say that (X, dX ) and (Y, dY ) are isometric if there exists an
isometry between them.

such that
                 dY (f (x), f (x0 )) < ε whenever dX (x, x0 ) < δ.
The function f is called continuous if it is continuous at every point x0 ∈ X.

excerpts.label: Definition 2.22
excerpts.text:
Definition 2.22 (Ultrametric space). A metric space (X, d) is an ultrametric
space if d satisfies the strong triangle inequality

              d(x, z) ≤ max{d(x, y), d(y, z)}     for all x, y, z ∈ X.

We would usually use u instead of d to denote an ultrametric.

excerpts.label: Proposition 2.23
excerpts.text:
Proposition 2.23. Let (X, u) be an ultrametric space. Then,
  1. If r > 0 and x, y ∈ X with u(x, y) < r, then Br (x) = Br (y).
  2. Any two open balls are either disjoint or one contains the other.
  3. Every triangle is isosceles, i.e., if x, y, z ∈ X, then at least two of the
     distances u(x, y), u(y, z), and u(z, x) are equal, and the third is less than
     or equal to the common value.

Example 2.24. Recall the definition of the Cantor set C ⊆ [0, 1]: it is con-
structed by repeatedly removing the open middle third from each interval. More
precisely, set C0 = [0, 1], and for each k ≥ 1, let Ck be the union of 2k closed in-
tervals obtained by removing the open middle third from each interval in Ck−1 .
The Cantor set is defined as
                                          ∞
                                          \
                                     C=      Ck .
                                        k=0

Equivalently, C consists of all numbers in [0, 1] whose base-3 expansion contains
only the digits 0 and 2. We endow the Cantor set C ⊆ [0, 1] with the ultrametric
as follows:
            (
              0     if x = y,
dC (x, y) =
               −n
              3     if x ̸= y and n = min{k ≥ 0 : x and y lie in different segments in Ck }.

above. It turns out that one can always create a nice visualization of ultrametric
spaces using trees. We will use this to help us understand ultrametric spaces
better. Although the following definition is for finite sets, it can be generalized
to infinite sets as well.

excerpts.label: Theorem 2.27
excerpts.text:
Theorem 2.27 (Finite dendrograms and ultrametrics are equivalent). Let X
be a finite set. Let D(X) be the set of dendrograms on X and U(X) be the set
of ultrametrics on X. There are two maps between D(X) and U(X) as follows:
  1. (From dendrogram to ultrametric) Given a dendrogram θ on X, define

      u(x, y) := inf{t ≥ 0 : x, y belong to the same block in θ(t)}    (x, y ∈ X).

      Then u is an ultrametric on X.
  2. (From ultrametric to dendrogram) Given an ultrametric u on X set, we
     define an equivalence relation ∼t for t ≥ 0,

                                x ∼t y ⇐⇒ u(x, y) ≤ t.

      Then we define θ by θ(t) := {[x]t : x ∈ X} where [x]t is the equivalence
      class of x under ∼t . This gives a dendrogram on X.
The above two maps, denoted by D : D(X) → U (X) and U : U(X) → D(X)
respectively, are inverses of each other.

previous example. The corresponding ultrametric u is given by
                           

                           

Conversely, starting from this ultrametric u, we can recover the original den-

excerpts.label: Example 3.6
excerpts.text:
Example 3.6. Every metric space is a topological space with the open sets
defined previously.
    As a special example, for R, every open ball is a bounded open interval
(a, b). Hence, every open set in R is a union of disjoint open intervals (including
unbounded intervals).
    Let (X, τ ) be a topological space. If there exists a metric d on X such that
open sets for d coincide with τ , we say (X, τ ) is metrizable.

Definition 3.13 (Basis). A basis B for a topology on a set X is a nonempty
family of subsets of X such that:
  1. For every x ∈ X, there exists some B ∈ B such that x ∈ B.

  2. If x ∈ B1 ∩ B2 with B1 , B2 ∈ B, then there exists B3 ∈ B with x ∈ B3 ⊆
     B1 ∩ B 2 .
The topology generated by B is: any U ⊂ X is open if for every x ∈ U , there
exists B ∈ B such that x ∈ B ⊆ U . Equivalently,

excerpts.label: Definition 3.26
excerpts.text:
Definition 3.26 (Closure Operation). Let X be a set and let

                                · : P(X) → P(X)

be a map. It is called a closure operation if for all A, B ⊂ X:

  (i) ∅ = ∅,
 (ii) A ⊂ A,
(iii) If D = A, then D = D,
 (iv) A ∪ B = A ∪ B.

   We now show that the closure operation and the topology we defined pre-
viously give rise to equivalent structures on a set. To this end, we identify the
notion of a closed set in a topological space first.

   • all open intervals (a, b) with a < b,

Example 3.40 (Order topology on {1, 2} × N (lexicographic) is not discrete).
Give X = {1, 2} × N the lexicographic order:

                (i, m) < (j, n)   iff i < j or (i = j and m < n).

Then (1, 1) is the least element. In the order topology, any basis element con-
taining (2, 1) is of the form (a, b) (or [ (1, 1), b)) with a < (2, 1) < b, and therefore
must contain some (1, n). Hence {(2, 1)} is not open, so the order topology on
X is not the discrete topology.

excerpts.label: Definition 3.41
excerpts.text:
Definition 3.41. Let (X, τX ) and (Y, τY ) be topological spaces. The product
topology on the product space X × Y is the topology generated by the basis
consisting of all products of open sets:

                        BX×Y = {U × V : U ∈ τX , V ∈ τY }.

Check: B is a basis. Note X × Y ∈ B so every point (x, y) ∈ X × Y lies in some
basis element.
   For U1 × V1 , U2 × V2 ∈ B, we have U1 ∩ U2 ∈ τX and V1 ∩ V2 ∈ τY , so

               (U1 × V1 ) ∩ (U2 × V2 ) = (U1 ∩ U2 ) × (V1 ∩ V2 ) ∈ B.



   Question: is B a topology? No, the union of basis elements is not necessarily
a basis element.
   It turns out that smaller bases can also generate the product topology.

Example 3.43
excerpts.text:
Example 3.43. Let X = Y = R with the standard topology. Then, B =
{(a, b) : a < b} is a basis for R. Hence, B × B = {(a, b) × (c, d) : a < b, c < d}
is a basis for the product topology on R2 . Note that (a, b) × (c, d) is an axis-
aligned open rectangle in R2 . Previously, we showed that this generates the same
topology as the one generated by open balls in R2 . So the product topology on
R2 is the same as the standard metric topology on R2 .
    We can inductively define the product topology on X1 × X2 × · · · × Xn for
any finite n. But things will be a bit different for infinite products. We will
discuss this later.

excerpts.label: Remark 3.52
excerpts.text:
Remark 3.52. The order and subspace topologies on a subset of a linearly or-
dered set need not agree. For instance, let Y = [0, 1)∪{2} ⊂ R with the induced
order. In the subspace topology, {2} is open in Y since {2} = (2 − 12 , 2 + 12 ) ∩ Y .
But in the order topology on Y , any basis element containing 2 is of the form
(a, 2]Y = {y ∈ Y : a < y ≤ 2} where a ∈ Y (because 2 is the greatest element of
Y ), so it contains points of Y strictly less than 2; hence {2} is not open there.

excerpts.label: Theorem 3.57
excerpts.text:
Let X and Y be topological spaces and let f : X → Y be a function. The following are equivalent:
1. f is continuous.
2. For all open sets H in Y, f^{−1}(H) is open in X.
3. For all closed sets C in Y, f^{−1}(C) is closed in X.
4. For all A ⊂ X, f(‾{A}) ⊆ ‾{f(A)} (This can be thought of as the Kuratowski definition of continuity).

excerpts.label: Theorem 3.64
excerpts.text:
Theorem 3.64.       1. (Constant function) If f : X → Y maps all of X to a
    single point y0 ∈ Y , then f is continuous.
  2. (Inclusion) If A is a subspace of X, the inclusion map i : A → X defined
     by i(a) = a is continuous.
  3. (Composition) If f : X → Y and g : Y → Z are continuous, then the
     composition g ◦ f : X → Z is continuous.
  4. (Restricting the domain) If f : X → Y is continuous and A ⊆ X, then
     the restriction f |A : A → Y defined by f |A (a) = f (a) is continuous.
  5. (Restricting or expanding the range) Let f : X → Y be continuous. If
     f (X) ⊂ Z ⊂ Y , then the function g : X → Z obtained by restricting the
     range of f is continuous. If Y ⊂ W , then the function h : iY →W ◦ f :
     X → W is continuous.

  6. (Local formulation) f : X → Y is continuous if X = ∪Uα for a family of
     open sets Uα and each restriction f |Uα is continuous.
  7. (Pasting lemma) If X = A ∪ B with A, B closed, and f : A → Y , g : B →
     Y are continuous and agree on A ∩ B (i.e., f (x) = g(x) for all x ∈ A ∩ B),
     then the function h : X → Y defined by
                                     (
                                       f (x), x ∈ A
                              h(x) =
                                       g(x), x ∈ B

        is continuous.

Example 3.82. Let X = RN = n≥1 R. Then, the “diagonal” map f : R → X
defined by f (t) = (t, t, t, . . .) is not continuous when X is endowed with the box
topology. Consider the open set (−1, 1)×(−1/2, 1/2)×(−1/3, 1/3)×· · · . Then,

          f −1 ((−1, 1) × (−1/2, 1/2) × (−1/3, 1/3) × · · · )
           = f −1 ((−1, 1) × R × · · · ∩ R × (−1/2, 1/2) × R × · · · ∩ · · · )
             \
           =      f −1 (R × · · · × (−1/n, 1/n) × · · · )
               n≥1
               \
           =       (−1/n, 1/n) = {0}.
               n≥1


Then f −1 ((−1, 1) × (−1/2, 1/2) × (−1/3, 1/3) × · · · ) is not open in R. Hence,
f is not continuous.
    This example actually gives us a hint how we can make things right. The
problem above is that when considering the arbitrary intersection of open sets,
we don’t get an open set. SO, we want things to be finite in some sense. This
leads to the following definition.

0} and let 0 = (0, 0, . . .). Then, 0 ∈ A: for any basis element U = (a1 , b1 ) ×
(a2 , b2 ) × · · · containing 0, we have that ai < 0 < bi for all i. So pick any point
(x1 , x2 , . . .) with xi ∈ (0, bi ) for all i, then (x1 , x2 , . . .) ∈ A ∩ U . So, A ∩ U ̸= ∅.

metric d. Let an = (x1n , x2n , . . .) be a sequence in A converging to 0. Then,
construct B = {(−x11 , x11 ) × (−x22 , x22 ) × · · · }. Then, 0 ∈ B but an ∈            / B for
all n ∈ N. So there exists a ball Br (0) ⊆ B for some r > 0 containing no point
in the sequence an . This is a contradiction. So RN with the box topology is not
metrizable.

excerpts.label: Example 3.96
excerpts.text:
Example 3.96. One can obtain a torus and a sphere via gluing/equivalence
relations.




  Figure 2: A torus and a sphere, illustrating the concept of quotient spaces.


    How can we get a topology on X ∗ from the topology on X? Recall that
the product topology can be characterized via some continuous maps. Maybe
we can do something similar here. A very natural map is the quotient map
p : X → X ∗ sending each point to its equivalence class.
    We of course want p to be continuous. That means we want a set of open
sets on X ∗ so that the preimage of each open set is open in X. We want to
make this topology as coarse as possible.

excerpts.label: Remark 3.98
excerpts.text:
Remark 3.98. The quotient topology is the finest topology on Y making q con-
tinuous: if τ is any topology on Y with q continuous, then τ ⊆ τq .

excerpts.label: Definition 3.99
excerpts.text:
Definition 3.99 (Quotient space). Let X be a topological space. Let ∼ be
an equivalence relation on X and let X ∗ := X/ ∼ be the set of equivalence
classes. The quotient space of X by ∼ is the set X ∗ endowed with the quotient
topology via the natural projection map p : X → X ∗ sending each point to its
equivalence class.

excerpts.label: Example 3.100
excerpts.text:
Example 3.100 (A 3–point quotient of R). Let p : R → Y = {−1, 0, 1} be
                               
                               −1, x < 0,
                               
                        p(x) = 0,      x = 0,
                               
                                 1,    x > 0.
                               

Endow Y with the quotient topology via p. A subset V ⊆ Y is open iff p−1 (V )
is open in R.
   • p−1 ({−1}) = (−∞, 0) and p−1 ({1}) = (0, ∞) are open ⇒ {−1}, {1} are
     open.
   • p−1 ({0}) = {0} is not open ⇒ {0} not open.
   • p−1 ({−1, 1}) = R \ {0} = (−∞, 0) ∪ (0, ∞) is open ⇒ {−1, 1} open.
   • p−1 ({−1, 0}) = (−∞, 0] and p−1 ({0, 1}) = [0, ∞) are not open.
   Thus
                    τY = {∅, {−1}, {1}, {−1, 1}, {−1, 0, 1}}.

excerpts.label: Definition 3.102
excerpts.text:
Definition 3.102. For two topological spaces X, Y and a surjective map q :
X → Y , we say q is a quotient map if

             a subset U ⊆ Y is open in Y iff q −1 (U ) is open in X.
   In other words, q is a quotient map if the topology on Y coincides with the
quotient topology via q.
   Whenever we have a quotient map q : X → Y , we can identify Y with
the quotient space X ∗ of X by the equivalence relation induced by q. More
precisely, we have the following proposition.

Example 3.105. Let X = [0, 2π] with the usual topology from R. Let Y =
S 1 = {(x, y) ∈ R2 : x2 + y 2 = 1} with the subspace topology from R2 . Define

                         p : X → Y,     p(t) = (cos t, sin t).

Then, p is surjective and continuous. p is not open unfortunately: [0, a) will not
be mapped to an open set. But p is closed. Later when we have more tools,
this can be proved easily. But now, let’s use techniques we have to prove it.

excerpts.label: Example 3.107
excerpts.text:
Example 3.107. Consider the subspace

  X = {(x, y) ∈ R2 : xy = 1} ∪ {(0, 0)} ⊂ R2 ,           q : X −→ R, q(x, y) = x.

The map q is surjective: for x ̸= 0 choose y = 1/x, and q(0, 0) = 0. It is
continuous as the restriction of the projection π1 : R2 → R.
   However q is not a quotient map. Indeed {(0, 0)} = Bε (0, 0) ∩ X for small
ε > 0, so {(0, 0)} is open in X. Thus

                        q −1 ({0}) = {(0, 0)} is open in X,

but {0} is not open in R. Hence the “only if” direction fails and q is not a
quotient map.
   The following theorem is analogous to the universal property of product
topology.

Theorem 3.108. Let q : X → Y be a quotient map and let Z be a topological
space. Let g : X → Z be such that g is constant on each fiber q −1 ({y}). This
induces a function f : Y → Z such that f ◦ q = g. Then
  1. f is continuous iff g is continuous.
  2. f is a quotient map iff g is a quotient map.

excerpts.label: Definition 3.110
excerpts.text:
Definition 3.110. Let f and g be continuous maps from a topological space
X to a topological space Y . We say that f and g are homotopic if there exists a
continuous map H : X ×[0, 1] → Y such that H(x, 0) = f (x) and H(x, 1) = g(x)
for all x ∈ X. H is called a homotopy between f and g. We write f ≃ g to
indicate that f and g are homotopic.

excerpts.label: Example 3.113
excerpts.text:
Example 3.113. More generally, if Y is a convex subset of some Rn and
f, g : X → Y are continuous, then

                         H(x, t) = (1 − t)f (x) + tg(x)

defines a homotopy f ≃ g. Thus any two maps into a convex (in particular,
contractible) space are homotopic. The target matters: regarded as maps S 1 →
D2 the identity and any constant map are homotopic, but as maps S 1 → S 1
they need not be. This is in fact quite nontrivial and we will return to it later.

Definition 3.116. Two spaces X and Y are homotopy equivalent if there exist
continuous maps f : X → Y and g : Y → X such that g◦f ≃ idX and f ◦g ≃ idY .
In this case f and g are homotopy inverses and we write X ≃ Y .

Remark 3.117. Homotopy equivalence is an equivalence relation on spaces. Any
homeomorphism is a homotopy equivalence (take g = f −1 ). The converse fails;
see the example below.
   One special case of homotopy equivalence is when one of the spaces is a
point.

Definition 3.118. A space X is contractible if the identity map idX is homo-
topic to a constant map cx0 : X → X sending every point to x0 . Equivalently,
there exists H : X × I → X with H(x, 0) = x and H(x, 1) = x0 for all x.

excerpts.text:
Example 3.122. S 1 is not contractible. We will prove this later.
   The contractible case is the trivial case of homotopy equivalence. More
generally, we can often find a smaller subspace which is homotopy equivalent to
the whole space. This is made precise by the following definitions.

excerpts.label: Definition 3.124
excerpts.text:
Definition 3.124. A subspace A ⊆ X is a deformation retract of X if there
is a retraction r : X → A such that there is a homotopy H : X × I → X with
H(x, 0) = x, H(x, 1) = r(x), and H(a, t) = a for all a ∈ A, t ∈ I. We call H a
deformation retraction.

excerpts.label: Proposition 3.125
excerpts.text:
Proposition 3.125. If A is a deformation retract of X then A ≃ X. Thus a
deformation retract gives a special homotopy equivalence (with inverse given by
the retraction).

excerpts.label: Example 3.127
excerpts.text:
Example 3.127. Not every retraction is a deformation retraction. In fact, for
any X and x0 ∈ X, the constant map cx0 : X → {x0 } is a retraction if {x0 } is
a retract of X, but it is a deformation retraction only if X is contractible.

Lemma 3.132 (Lifting lemma). Let p : R → S 1 be p(t) = eit . If f : S 1 → S 1
is homotopic to a constant map, than f lifts, i.e., there exists a continuous
f˜ : S 1 → R with p ◦ f˜ = f .

if it is a homeomorphism onto its image f (X) (with the subspace topology
inherited from Y ). In particular, f is injective.

excerpts.label: Definition 3.136
excerpts.text:
Definition 3.136. Let X and Y be two disjoint topological spaces. Then, the
disjoint union of X and Y is the topological space

                                      X ⊔Y

whose underlying set is the disjoint union of sets X and Y and whose topology
is given by

    U ⊆ X ⊔ Y is open ⇐⇒ U ∩ X is open in X and U ∩ Y is open in Y.

Equivalently, the topology is given by

                       τX⊔Y = {U ⊔ V | U ∈ τX , V ∈ τY }.

excerpts.label: Theorem 3.140
excerpts.text:
Theorem 3.140 (Common deformation–retract envelope). For topological spaces
X and Y , the following are equivalent:
  1. X and Y are homotopy equivalent.

  2. There exists a space Z and embeddings iX : X ,→ Z, iY : Y ,→ Z such
     that iX (X) and iY (Y ) are each deformation retracts of Z (possibly via
     two different homotopies).

excerpts.label: Definition 4.2
excerpts.text:
Definition 4.2. A sequence (xn )n∈N in a topological space X is said to converge
to a point x ∈ X if for every neighbourhood U of x, there exists N ∈ N such
that xn ∈ U for all n ≥ N .

Example 4.5. Let X = R be endowed with the countable complement topology:
a set U ⊆ X is open iff X \ U is countable or U = ∅.
   • Any sequence (xn ) converging to x is eventually equal to x. Indeed, we
     let B = {xn : xn ̸= x} and hence U = X \ B is an open neighborhood of
     x. Then, there exists N such that xn ∈ U for all n ≥ N , i.e., xn ∈
                                                                       / B for
     all n ≥ N . This means that xn = x for all n ≥ N .
   • The closed sets are exactly the countable sets and X itself. Hence, if
     A ⊊ X is uncountable, then A = X.

   Thus [0, 1] = R, but there is no sequence in [0, 1] converging to 2.

Example 4.7. Let X be endowed with the trivial topology τ = {∅, X}. Then
the constant sequence (xn ) with xn = a ∈ X for all n ∈ N converges to every
point in X.

excerpts.label: Definition 4.12
excerpts.text:
Definition 4.12. A set Λ is a directed set if it is a non-empty set with a relation
≤ such that
   • reflexive: for all λ ∈ Λ, λ ≤ λ,
   • transitive: for all λ1 , λ2 , λ3 ∈ Λ, if λ1 ≤ λ2 and λ2 ≤ λ3 , then λ1 ≤ λ3 ,

   • directed: for all λ1 , λ2 ∈ Λ, there exists µ ∈ Λ such that λ1 ≤ µ and
     λ2 ≤ µ.
   This relation ≤ is called a direction on Λ.

excerpts.label: Remark 4.13
excerpts.text:
Remark 4.13. Note a direction may not be a partial order, i.e., it may not be
antisymmetric. For example, let Λ = {a, b} with a ≤ b and b ≤ a. This is a
directed set but not a poset because a ̸= b.

Example 4.18. Let P denote the collection of all finite partitions of the closed
interval [a, b] into closed subintervals. In other words, each P ∈ P has the form
P = {[x0 , x1 ], [x1 , x2 ], . . . , [xn−1 , xn ]} where a = x0 < x1 < · · · < xn = b.
    This becomes a directed set if we define the direction by refinement: for two
partitions P1 , P2 ∈ P, we say that P1 ≤ P2 if P2 is a refinement of P1 (i.e., every
subinterval in P1 is a union of subintervals in P2 ).
    Now, consider a function f : [a, b] → R. Define a net (RL (P ))P ∈P as follows:
for each partition P = {[x0 , x1 ], [x1 , x2 ], . . . , [xn−1 , xn ]}, let
                                n
                                X
                    RL (P ) =             inf         f (x) · (xi − xi−1 ).
                                      x∈[xi−1 ,xi ]
                                i=1

This net is called the lower Riemann sum net of f .
   Similarly, we can define the upper Riemann sum net (RU (P ))P ∈P by
                                n
                                X
                    RU (P ) =             sup         f (x) · (xi − xi−1 ).
                                i=1 x∈[xi−1 ,xi ]

    If both nets converge to the same limit L, then we say that f is Riemann
integrable on [a, b] with integral L.

excerpts.label: Example 4.19
excerpts.text:
Example 4.19. One typical example of a net is the following: let X be a
topological space and x ∈ X. Let Λ be the set of all neighbourhoods of x
and define the direction on Λ by U ≤ V iff V ⊆ U (reverse inclusion). You
should check that this is indeed a directed set. Pick a point xU ∈ U for each
neighbourhood U of x. Then the net (xU )U ∈Λ converges to x. To see this, let
V be any neighbourhood of x, then for all U ≥ V , we have xU ∈ U ⊆ V . This
shows that xU → x.

excerpts.label: Example 5.6
excerpts.text:
Example 5.6. Let X = R. Then, the complement finite topology on X is not
first countable. To see this, suppose there is a countable basis of neighbourhoods
{Bn : n ∈ N} at some point x ∈ S    X. Since each Bn is open, we have X \ Bn
is finite for each n. Let E = x ∪ n∈N (X \ Bn ). Then, E is countable. Now,
pick any y ∈ R \ E and consider the open set U = X \ {y}. Note that U is a
neighbourhood of x. However, for any n, we have Bn ̸⊆ U since y ∈ Bn \ U .
This contradicts the assumption that {Bn : n ∈ N} is a basis at x. Hence, X is
not first countable.

excerpts.label: Theorem 5.8
excerpts.text:
Theorem 5.8. Let X be a topological space.

   1. For A ⊆ X and x ∈ X, if there is a sequence (an ) ⊆ A with an → x,
      then x ∈ A. If X is first countable, the converse holds: x ∈ A implies that
      there exists a sequence (an ) ⊆ A with an → x.
   2. If f : X → Y is continuous at x and xn → x in X, then f (xn ) → f (x) in
      Y . If X is first countable, the converse holds: xn → x ⇒ f (xn ) → f (x)
      for all sequences (xn ) in X implies that f is continuous at x.

excerpts.label: Definition 5.27
excerpts.text:
Definition 5.27. Let X be a topological space such that one-point sets are
closed. We say that X is:
  1. regular if for any point x and a disjoint closed set B, there exist disjoint
     open sets U and V such that x ∈ U and B ⊆ V .
  2. normal if for any two disjoint closed sets A and B, there exist disjoint
     open sets U and V such that A ⊆ U and B ⊆ V .

excerpts.label: Lemma 5.30
excerpts.text:
Lemma 5.30. Let X be a topological space with one-point sets closed. Then,
  1. X is regular iff for every neighbourhood U of a any point x, there exists a
     neighbourhood V of x such that x ∈ V ⊂ V ⊂ U .

  2. X is normal iff for every closed set A and any open set U such that
     A ⊂ U ⊆ X, there exists an open V with A ⊂ V ⊂ V ⊂ U .

Example 6.10. {1/n}n∈N ⊂ R is not compact: {{1/n}} is an open cover with
no finite subcover.

exists U ∈ U such that 0 ∈ U . Choose ε > 0 such that (−ε, ε) ⊂ U . Then,
only finitely many points of the set {1/n}n∈N are outside U . Choosing open
sets from U covering these finitely many points gives a finite subcover.

excerpts.label: Example 6.35
excerpts.text:
Example 6.35 (Compact but not sequentially compact). Let X = {0, 1}[0,1]
with the product topology. By Tychonoff, X is compact. For each n ∈ N
define fn ∈ X by fn (r) = the n-th binary digit of r (choose the expansion not
ending in all 1’s). Take any subsequence (fnk ). If it converges, we know that for
any r ∈ [0, 1], the sequence (fnk (r)) must converge in [0, 1]. Choose r ∈ [0, 1]
whose binary expansion has digit nk equal to 0 if k is odd and 1 if k is even
(this is possible since we prescribe digits only on the positions {nk }). Then
fnk (r) = 0, 1, 0, 1, . . . does not converge. Therefore (fnk ) cannot converge in the
product topology. Hence no subsequence of (fn ) converges; X is not sequentially
compact.

φ : Γ → Λ is an increasing function between directed sets Γ and Λ such that: For

then the subnet can be represented as (xλγ ) or (xφ(γ) ) (cf. the subsequence
notation (xnk )).

since C = Cn where each Cn is closed.

between C and {0, 2}N : each x ∈ C can be written in base 3 using only digits
0 and 2, and this gives a bijection between C and {0, 2}N . It turns out that
this bijection is actually a homeomorphism. To see this, let’s actually give a
metric on {0, 2}N that induces the product topology. For any two sequences
(an ), (bn ) ∈ {0, 2}N , define

{0, 2}N is actually the same as the ultrametric on C under the above bijection.

excerpts.label: Example 6.53
excerpts.text:
Example 6.53. RN is not locally compact. For any x ∈ RN , pick any basic
open neighborhood U = U1 × U2 × · · · × Un × R × R × · · · . Suppose there
exists some compact set K such that U ⊂ K. Consider the projection map
πn+1 : RN → R defined by πn+1 ((xi )) = xn+1 . Then, πn+1 (U ) = R and hence
πn+1 (K) ⊃ πn+1 (U ) = R. However, the continuous image of a compact set is
compact and R is not compact. This is a contradiction. Therefore, there does
not exist any compact set K such that U ⊂ K and hence RN is not locally
compact.

excerpts.label: Theorem 6.54
excerpts.text:
Theorem 6.54. Let X be a topological space. Then, X is locally compact
Hausdorff iff there exists a compact Hausdorff space Y such that

   • X is a subspace of Y ;
   • Y \ X consists of a single point.
Such a space Y is called the one-point compactification of X and is unique up
to homeomorphism.

excerpts.label: Definition 6.67
excerpts.text:
Definition 6.67. Let U = {Uα }α∈A be an open cover of a topological space X.
A partition of unity subordinated to U is a collection of continuous functions
{φα : X → [0, 1]}α∈A such that:
   • supp ϕα ⊂ Uα ; here the support of a function f : X → R is defined as
     supp f = {x ∈ X : f (x) ̸= 0}
   • {supp φα } is locally finite; and
   • For every x ∈ X, α∈A φα (x) = 1.
                        P

excerpts.label: Lemma 6.68
excerpts.text:
Lemma 6.68. Let X be Hausdorff and paracompact. Then, every open cover
U = {Uα }α∈J of X has a shrinking, i.e., an open refinement {Vα }α∈J covering
X such that Vα ⊂ Uα for each α.

excerpts.label: Theorem 7.1
excerpts.text:
Theorem 7.1 (Intermediate Value Theorem). Let f : [0, 1] → R be a continuous
function. WLOG, we assume that f (0) < f (1). Then, for any r ∈ [f (0), f (1)],
there exists c ∈ (0, 1) such that f (c) = r.
    This is a consequence of the fact that [0, 1] is “connected”.

excerpts.text:
Definition 7.2. Let X be a topological space. A separation of X is a pair
of disjoint nonempty open sets U, V ⊆ X with X = U ∪ V . The space X is
disconnected if it admits a separation; otherwise X is connected.

Example 7.14. RN with box topology is not connected. Indeed, let

       U = {all bounded sequences},          V = {all unbounded sequences}.

Then, U and V are disjoint, nonempty and U ∪ V = RN . Given a ∈ RN , note
that (a1 −1, a1 +1)×(a2 −1, a2 +1)×· · · is an open neighborhood of a contained
in U (resp. V ) is a is bounded (resp. unbounded). Hence, U and V are open
in the box topology, so they separate RN .

excerpts.label: Definition 7.16
excerpts.text:
Definition 7.16. A linear poset L having more than one element is called a
linear continuum if the following hold:
   1. L has the least upper bound property: every nonempty subset of L that
      is bounded above has a least upper bound. (sup exists)
   2. If x < y, then there exists z ∈ L such that x < z < y.

excerpts.label: Definition 7.25
excerpts.text:
Definition 7.25. Let X be a topological space. We define an equivalence
relation on X by declaring x ∼ y iff there exists a connected subspace of X
containing both x and y. The equivalence classes of this relation are called the
components of X.
    We define another equivalence relation on X by declaring x ≈ y iff there
exists a path in X connecting x and y. The equivalence classes of this relation
are called the path components of X.
   Symmetry and relexivity are clear. For transitivity, if x, y lie in a connected
subspace A and y, z lie in a connected subspace B, then x, z lie in the connected
subspace A ∪ B (since y ∈ A ∩ B).

Remark 7.28. Each component of X is closed as its closure is connected. If X
has only finitely many components, then each component is also open, since its
complement is a finite union of closed sets. This doesn’t hold in general for
infinitely many components.

excerpts.label: Unnumbered: Subsets, power sets and complements
excerpts.text:
Set calculus A set A is a subset of a set B if every element of A is also an
element of B. We write A ⊆ B to denote that A is a subset of B. If A is a
subset of B but not equal to B, we say that A is a proper subset of B and denote
it by A ⊊ B.
    We let P(A) denote the power set of A, which is the set of all subsets of A.
    We say two sets A and B are equal if they have the same elements, that is,
if A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A. We write A = B to denote that A and B are equal.
    We let A\B denote the set difference of A and B, which is the set of elements
in A that are not in B. Formally, A\B = {x ∈ A : x ∈    / B}. When B ⊆ A, we
say A\B is the complement of B in A.
    The empty set, denoted ∅, is a set that contains no elements. It is a subset
of every set.

A × B, is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) where a ∈ A and b ∈ B:

   Formally, an ordered pair can be defined as follows and define the cartesian
product as a set of sets:
                            (a, b) := {{a}, {a, b}}.

excerpts.label: Unnumbered: Equality and comparison of cardinality
excerpts.text:
For any two sets A and B, we say they have the same cardinality if there exists
a bijection f : A → B. Intuitively, this means that the sets “have the same
number of elements”.
    Having the same cardinality is an equivalence relation on the class of all sets.
    We write |A| = |B| to denote that the sets A and B have the same cardinality.
    We say A has cardinality less than or equal to B (or B has cardinality greater
than or equal to A), denoted |A| ≤ |B| or |B| ≥ |A|, if there exists an injection
f : A → B.

excerpts.label: Unnumbered: Continuity of real functions
excerpts.text:
For real functions f : R → R, we have the notion of continuity using ε-δ defini-
tion: a function f : R → R is continuous at a point x0 ∈ R if for every ε > 0
there exists δ > 0 such that

                    |f (x) − f (x0 )| < ε   whenever |x − x0 | < δ.

We also have the notion of continuity using sequences: a function f : R → R is
continuous at a point x0 ∈ R if for every sequence (xn ) in R converging to x0 ,
the sequence (f (xn )) converges to f (x0 ).

Here is some simple criterion for quotient maps. A map is said to be open
if the image of every open set is open. Similarly, a map is said to be closed if
the image of every closed set is closed.
